title: Which of the following class of statement usually produces no
subject: Compiler Design
text: Which of the following class of statement usually produces no executable code when compiled?
solution:
Concept

A compiler classifies source statements into two broad kinds. Non-executable (declarative) statements only give the compiler information — names, types, sizes, scope — so it can reserve storage and check usage; they translate to no machine instructions that run at execution time. Executable statements describe actions to be carried out at run time, so the compiler emits actual machine code for them.

Applying it here

“declaration” is a declarative statement: it tells the compiler the type and storage requirement of an identifier. The compiler uses it to build its symbol table and lay out memory, but it usually emits no run-time instruction for the declaration itself. Hence it is the class that normally produces no executable code.

Contrast with the other classes

  • “assignment statements” — compute a value and store it into a location; the compiler must emit load/compute/store instructions that run at execution time.

  • “input and output statements” — transfer data to or from devices/streams, which requires run-time calls and instructions.

  • “structural statements” — control statements such as branches and loops; they compile into jump/test instructions that direct the flow at run time.

Cross-check

Note the standard distinction between a declaration and a definition: a pure declaration merely introduces a name, whereas a definition that initialises storage may emit code. The question asks for the class that “usually” produces no executable code, which matches a plain declaration.

optionFeedback.html: “declaration” only supplies type and storage information to the compiler for its symbol table and memory layout, so it normally yields no run-time machine instruction — it fits a class that produces no executable code.

“assignment statements” perform a computation and write the result into a location at run time, so the compiler must emit instructions for them — this is an executable action, not a purely informational statement.
“input and output statements” move data to or from external streams or devices during execution, which needs run-time instructions, so they do generate executable code.
“structural statements” are control constructs (branches, loops) that steer program flow at run time; they compile into jump and test instructions, so they are executable.

title: Which of the following is the CORRECT sequence of the

text: Which of the following is the CORRECT sequence of the phases of a compiler?

solution:
Concept: A compiler transforms source code into target code through a fixed pipeline in which each phase consumes the previous phase's output: lexical analysis (characters -> tokens), syntax analysis (tokens -> parse tree), semantic analysis (type/scope checking), intermediate code generation (parse tree -> intermediate representation), code optimization (improves that intermediate representation), and code generation (intermediate representation -> target code).

Application: Trace the five phases named in this item through that dependency chain:

  1. Lexical analysis must run first, since it is the only one of these phases that reads raw source characters.

  2. Syntax analysis runs next, because it needs the token stream that lexical analysis produces.

  3. Intermediate code generation runs after syntax analysis, since it needs a validated parse tree as its input.

  4. Code optimization runs after intermediate code generation, because it improves the intermediate representation that phase produces.

  5. Code generation runs last, emitting target code from the optimized intermediate form.

So the order among these five phases is: lexical analysis, syntax analysis, intermediate code generation, code optimization, code generation.

Cross-check: Reading the dependencies backward confirms it: code generation needs the optimized intermediate code, which needs the unoptimized intermediate code from intermediate code generation, which needs the parse tree from syntax analysis, which needs the tokens from lexical analysis -- a clean chain with no phase used before its input exists. (Semantic analysis, which normally sits between syntax analysis and intermediate code generation, is not among the phases listed in these options.)

optionFeedback.html: In this listing, code generation is placed right after intermediate code generation, with code optimization coming last. Think again about how code optimization and code generation relate to each other here -- one of them works on the compiler's intermediate representation and the other emits the compiler's final output, and only one order between the two lets each phase have valid input to work with.

In this listing, intermediate code generation is placed before syntax analysis, and code optimization is placed after code generation. Think again about what each of these five phases needs as its input -- only one arrangement lets every phase consume something that already exists by the time it runs.

In this listing, intermediate code generation is placed before syntax analysis. Think again about what intermediate code generation needs as its input, and about which earlier phase in this list is responsible for producing that input.

text: When a compiler runs on one machine and produces code for a different machine, this is called:
solution:
Concept

A compiler is classified by the relationship between the machine it runs on (the host) and the machine its generated code is meant to run on (the target). When host and target are the same platform, the compiler is called a native compiler. When host and target differ — for example, compiling on an x86 desktop to produce code for an ARM microcontroller — the compiler is called a cross compiler, and the process is cross compilation.

Application

  1. The stem describes exactly this host/target split: "runs on one machine" (the host) and "produces code for a different machine" (the target).

  2. This host-vs-target distinction is precisely the definition of a cross compiler, so the compiling activity described is cross compilation.

  3. "One pass" and "two pass" instead classify a compiler by how many times it scans/traverses the source program during translation — a completely different axis (single-machine internal architecture) that says nothing about whether the host and target machines differ.

  4. Since cross compilation directly and uniquely matches the stem's description, "None of the above" does not apply.

Cross-check

Real-world toolchains confirm this: GCC and LLVM/Clang both document a "host" (machine running the compiler) and a "target" (machine the generated code runs on); when a single toolchain build sets these to different architectures, its documentation calls it a cross compiler. This matches option 0 and rules out the pass-count based distractors, which describe an unrelated property of the compiler.

optionFeedback.html: Cross compilation names the setup where the compiler executes on a host machine while the object code it emits is meant to run on a target machine whose instruction set or platform differs from the host's.
One pass compilation names a compiler architecture that scans the source program a single time, performing lexical analysis, parsing, and code generation together within that single traversal.

Two pass compilation names a compiler architecture that scans the source program across two separate traversals — typically one pass to build tables and perform analysis, and a second pass to generate the target code.

title: The action of parsing the source program into proper syntactic
subject: Compiler Design
text: The action of parsing the source program into proper syntactic classes is known as
solution:
Correct answer: Syntax analysis

Explanation: Parsing the source program into proper syntactic classes means taking the stream of tokens and organizing them according to the grammar to produce a parse tree or abstract syntax tree. This process is called syntax analysis (parsing).

  • Lexical analysis: converts the raw character stream into tokens (identifiers, keywords, literals, operators). It does not build syntactic structures.

  • Syntax analysis: takes tokens and builds the parse tree or abstract syntax tree according to the language grammar. This is the parsing step.

  • Semantic analysis: checks meaning, type correctness, and scope on the AST produced by syntax analysis.

  • Intermediate code generation: produces an intermediate representation from the AST for optimization or final code generation; this occurs after parsing and semantic checks.

Therefore, the correct term for 'parsing the source program into proper syntactic classes' is syntax analysis.

Syntax analysis (parsing) takes the sequence of tokens produced by lexical analysis and builds a syntactic structure (parse tree or abstract syntax tree) according to the language grammar. This is the phase that organizes tokens into grammatical classes and hierarchical constructs.
Incorrect. Lexical analysis groups characters into lexemes and produces tokens (identifiers, keywords, literals, operators). It does not perform parsing or build grammatical structures from tokens.

Incorrect. Semantic analysis checks the meaning of the syntactic constructs (for example, type checking and scope resolution) after the syntax analysis has produced a parse tree or AST. It does not perform the parsing into syntactic classes.

Incorrect. Intermediate code generation is a later compiler phase that translates the verified AST into an intermediate representation for optimization or target code generation. It does not parse the source into syntactic classes.

title: Which of the following grammar can be used to design
subject: Compiler Design
text: Which of the following grammar can be used to design Lexical Analysis of Compiler?
solution:
Lexical analysis describes tokens using regular languages, so regular grammar is exactly sufficient and is the natural formalism for specifying a lexer.

However, any language that can be generated by a regular grammar can also be generated by more powerful grammars such as context-free or recursively enumerable grammars. This means those grammars can, in principle, also be used to describe the same token languages, even though they are more expressive than needed.

  • Regular grammar: directly models regular expressions and finite automata used in lexical analyzers, and is the minimal and standard choice for token specification.

  • Context-free grammar: strictly more powerful than regular grammars and capable of generating all regular languages, so it can describe the same token patterns but is typically used for syntax analysis rather than for implementing lexical analyzers.

  • Recursively enumerable grammar: the most general class in the Chomsky hierarchy and also capable of generating all regular languages, so it can in principle specify lexical tokens, but is far more complex than necessary and not used in practical lexer design.

In summary, all three listed grammars can theoretically be used to design the lexical analysis phase because they can generate regular languages, but regular grammar is the appropriate and sufficient choice for real lexical analyzers, while context-free and recursively enumerable grammars are unnecessarily powerful for this purpose.

title: Which of the following option having lexical error?
subject: Compiler Design
text: Which of the following option having lexical error?
solution:
Correct answer: int 3y12 — variable names cannot start with a digit, so this is a lexical error.

  • int float; The lexer produces valid keyword tokens ('int' and 'float'). The issue is that a keyword is being used where an identifier is expected, which the parser will flag as a syntactic error. This is not a lexical error.

  • int x = 2; This is lexically and syntactically correct: tokens include the keyword 'int', identifier 'x', the assignment symbol, numeric literal '2', and a semicolon. It is a valid declaration with initialization.

  • int 3y12 This is a lexical error because identifiers cannot begin with a digit. The lexer cannot form a valid identifier token from '3y12' (it would start a numeric token at '3' and then encounter letters), so lexical analysis fails.

  • int y = y/0; This is lexically and syntactically valid: tokens and structure are correct. Division by zero is a runtime or semantic error (undefined behavior in many languages), not a lexical error. Also beware of using y before it is initialized.

The error (if any) arises when the parser expects an identifier but finds a keyword; that is a syntactic error (you cannot use a reserved keyword as a variable name).

int x = 2; — This is lexically and syntactically correct. The lexer recognizes 'int', identifier 'x', '=', numeric literal '2', and ';' as valid tokens; the statement is a valid declaration with initialization.

int 3y12 — This is a lexical error because identifiers cannot start with a digit. The lexer cannot produce a valid identifier token for '3y12'; instead it would start a numeric token at '3' and then encounter invalid characters for that token. Therefore this fails at lexical analysis.

Answer: DFA can be used for designing a lexical analyzer.

Why this is correct: Lexical patterns are regular languages, and regular expressions that describe tokens can be converted into deterministic finite automata for efficient scanning.

title: In lexical analysis, pattern is generally described using
subject: Compiler Design
text: In lexical analysis, a pattern is generally described using __________.
solution:
In lexical analysis, a pattern is generally described using Regular Expressions (Regex).

How it Works

A lexical analyzer reads the source code character-by-character and groups them into meaningful units called lexemes (like keywords, identifiers, operators, or literals).

  • A Lexeme is the actual text string (e.g., 125, totalCount, if).

  • A Token is the abstract category assigned to that string (e.g., NUMBER, IDENTIFIER, KEYWORD).

  • A Pattern is the descriptive rule that dictates what characters can form a given token.

These patterns are defined mathematically and practically using Regular Expressions. For example:

  • An identifier pattern might be written as: [a-zA-Z_][a-zA-Z0-9_]* (starts with a letter or underscore, followed by any number of alphanumeric characters).

  • A digit/number pattern might be written as: [0-9]+.

During the generation of a compiler, these regular expressions are converted behind the scenes into Finite Automata (specifically Deterministic Finite Automata, or DFAs) to physically execute the matching process on the input text.

incorrect.Context-free grammars describe syntax for parsing, not lexical patterns. Review the distinction between regular languages used in lexing and context-free languages for parsing.

title: Which of the following features cannot be captured by CFG.
subject: Compiler Design
text: Which of the following features cannot be captured by a CFG.

options.html: Whether a variable is declared before its use

solution:
Key idea: Context-free grammars (CFGs) generate languages by rewriting single nonterminals and can express recursive and nested syntactic structures, but they cannot enforce context-sensitive relationships that require matching or comparing identifiers across distant parts of a program.

  • Syntax of a recursive procedures: Can be captured by a CFG. A production can include the same nonterminal to model recursion, allowing arbitrarily deep recursive structures.

  • Syntax of if-then-else statements: Can be captured by a CFG. Nesting of conditionals is context-free; grammar ambiguities such as the dangling-else are resolved by grammar design or parser rules.

  • Whether a variable is declared before its use: Cannot be captured by a CFG. This is a context-sensitive semantic requirement that needs tracking of declarations and scopes (for example via a symbol table) and comparing identifier identities across different parts of the program.

  • Matching nested parentheses: Can be captured by a CFG. Balanced nesting is the classic example of a context-free language (e.g., S -> '(' S ')' S | ε).

Therefore, the feature that cannot be captured by a CFG is whether a variable is declared before its use.

optionFeedback.html: A context-free grammar can describe recursive constructs because productions may be defined in terms of the nonterminal itself, allowing arbitrarily deep recursion. For example, a procedure body nonterminal can expand to include calls to the same procedure form.

If-then-else syntax can be captured by a CFG, including nested conditionals. Note that ambiguities such as the dangling-else are grammar issues that can be resolved by adjusting productions or parser precedence, not by rejecting CFG as a model.

Ensuring a variable is declared before its use is a context-sensitive semantic property that requires tracking declarations across scope (e.g., symbol tables). CFGs cannot enforce such cross-references or identity checks; this requires context-sensitive analysis during semantic checking.

Matching nested parentheses is the canonical example of a context-free language. A CFG can generate all correctly nested parentheses (for example, S -> '(' S ')' S | ε), so this structure is within the expressive power of CFGs.

title: Consider the grammar. SxSxS For string “xxxxxx”, How many total
subject: Compiler Design
text:
Consider the grammar.
S -> SxSxS | ϵ
For a string “xxxxxx”, How many total number of parse tree/s are possible.
solution:
Key insight: each application of the rule S -> S x S x S adds two terminal symbols 'x'.

Step 1: Determine how many times the rule must be applied.

  • Let k be the number of times S -> S x S x S is used. Each use contributes 2 x's, so 2k = 6, giving k = 3.

Step 2: Count the number of distinct parse trees for k = 3.

  • Each internal node of the parse tree has exactly three ordered children (a full ordered ternary tree). The number of such trees with k internal nodes is given by the Fuss–Catalan (generalized Catalan) formula:

  • Number = 1/((3-1)k + 1) * binomial(3k, k) = 1/(2k + 1) * C(3k, k).

  • For k = 3: binomial(9, 3) = 84, and 2k + 1 = 7, so the number = 84 / 7 = 12.

Conclusion: There are 12 distinct parse trees that generate the string "xxxxxx".

title: Find the Ambiguous CFG.
subject: Compiler Design
text: Find the Ambiguous CFG.
solution:
Answer: The ambiguous grammar is S → 1S | S0 | 2.

Explanation and explicit ambiguity example:

  • Two different leftmost derivations for the string 120 show ambiguity:

  1. Derivation 1 (use production that adds a leading 1 first): S ⇒ 1S ⇒ 1 S0 ⇒ 1 2 0

  2. Derivation 2 (use production that adds a trailing 0 first): S ⇒ S0 ⇒ 1S0 ⇒ 1 2 0

These two derivations produce the same terminal string but have different parse-tree shapes, so the grammar S → 1S | S0 | 2 is ambiguous.

Why the other grammars are unambiguous:

  • Grammar S → 1S | 0S | 2: This generates strings by repeatedly prepending a 1 or 0 until the base 2 is produced (strings of the form (1|0)*2). For any final string, the sequence of prepended symbols is exactly the prefix before 2, so the derivation is unique.

  • Grammar S → 1S0 | 2: This generates strings of the form 1^n 2 0^n. The number of recursive steps n is fixed by the counts of 1s and 0s in the string, so there is exactly one derivation for each string.

Conclusion: S → 1S | S0 | 2 is ambiguous (example: 120). The other two listed grammars are unambiguous.

This grammar is unambiguous. It generates strings by repeatedly prepending a 1 or 0 until you reach 2 (for example, 1012 arises as S ⇒ 1S ⇒ 10S ⇒ 101S ⇒ 1012). For any resulting string, the sequence of prepended symbols is fixed, so there is a unique parse tree.

This grammar is unambiguous. It produces strings of the form 1^n 2 0^n (apply S → 1S0 n times, then S → 2). The number n is uniquely determined by the counts of 1s and 0s, so each string has exactly one derivation and one parse tree.

title: Which of the following is true AS aXb aAbS aAb
subject: Compiler Design
text:
Which of the following is true :
G1: S → AS | ε
A → axb | ε
G2: S → aAbS | ε
A → aAb | ε

(a, b and x are all terminal symbols; S and A are the only non-terminals.)

options.html: G1 is LR(1) while G2 is not LR(1)
There exists a string in the language of G1 for which G1 has an infinite number of parse trees.

solution:
Concept

A grammar is ambiguous when some string in its language has two or more distinct parse trees (equivalently, two or more distinct leftmost derivations) — even one such string is enough, and infinitely many parse trees for one string still counts as ambiguous.

Two grammars are equivalent only if they generate exactly the same language; a single string produced by one but not the other already disproves equivalence.

Every LR(1) grammar admits a unique deterministic parse for each string, so an ambiguous grammar can never be LR(1).

Application

  1. Trace ε through G1: S → ε directly gives one parse tree. S → AS with A → ε then S → ε gives a second, distinct tree. Repeating S → AS any number of times, using A → ε at each step before the final S → ε, gives a further distinct tree for every repetition count — all yielding the same string ε. So G1 already has infinitely many parse trees for ε alone, which makes it ambiguous and confirms that the statement about an infinite number of parse trees for some string of G1 holds.

  2. Compare the languages: in G1, A → axb | ε lets A produce the terminal string "axb" (a, x and b are all terminals), so "axb" belongs to L(G1). G2's productions (S → aAbS | ε, A → aAb | ε) only ever combine the terminals a and b, so no string containing x can ever appear in L(G2). The two languages therefore differ, so the two grammars are not equivalent.

  3. Check G2 for ambiguity: each application of S → aAbS (or A → aAb) nests one matching a…b pair around whatever comes next, and the only way to stop is A → ε or the final S → ε — there is no way to insert an extra ε-step without changing the resulting string, so every string of G2 has exactly one derivation. G2 is therefore not ambiguous, so the claim that both grammars are ambiguous does not hold — only G1 is. For example, take the string "ab": the only way to produce it is S → aAbS with A → ε (contributing nothing between a and b) and the trailing S → ε (contributing nothing after b) — any other choice for A or the trailing S adds more terminal symbols and yields a longer string, so "ab" has exactly one derivation, not two.

  4. Since G1 is ambiguous, and an ambiguous grammar can never be LR(1), G1 cannot be LR(1) — so the claim that G1 is LR(1) while G2 is not fails immediately, regardless of G2's own LR(1) status.

Cross-check

Re-deriving axb in G1 (S → AS → (axb)S, then the trailing S is terminated with S → ε) confirms it belongs to L(G1); and it too has infinitely many parse trees, not just ε — extra A → ε steps can be inserted before or after the A → axb occurrence any number of times without changing the resulting string, exactly like the ε case. This is consistent with G1 being ambiguous purely because of its unrestricted ε-recursion in S → AS, and with G2's strictly nested a…b matching giving every string a unique derivation.

Result: "Both are not equivalent" and "There exists a string in the language of G1 for which G1 has an infinite number of parse trees" are TRUE; "Both are ambiguous" and "G1 is LR(1) while G2 is not LR(1)" are FALSE.

optionFeedback.html: This treats the two grammars as behaving the same way, but they do not: the first grammar admits more than one distinct derivation for some strings it generates, while the second grammar's structure fixes exactly one derivation for every string it can produce. So it is not true that both grammars are ambiguous — only one of them is.

The two grammars generate different languages. In the first grammar, A → axb | ε (a, x, b are terminals) lets the string "axb" belong to its language, while the second grammar's productions only ever combine the terminals a and b and can never produce a string containing x — so the languages are not the same.

This assumes the first grammar could still be deterministically parsed even though it is ambiguous — but no ambiguous grammar can be LR(1), since LR(1) parsing requires a single deterministic parse for every string. Since the first grammar is ambiguous, it cannot be LR(1), which already makes this claim false regardless of the second grammar's own LR(1) status.

There exist strings — in particular the empty string ε — for which the first grammar has infinitely many distinct parse trees: ε can come from S → ε directly, or from S → AS with A → ε followed by S → ε, or from repeating S → AS any number of times with A → ε at each step — every repetition count gives a distinct parse tree yielding the same string ε.

title: Which of the following features cannot be captured by CFG?
subject: Compiler Design
text: Which of the following features cannot be captured by CFG?
solution:
Summary: The features that cannot be captured by a context-free grammar are matching of function arguments and declaration of a variable; these require semantic/context-sensitive checks.

  • Syntax of nested if-else: Can be specified by a CFG. Nested constructs are syntactic and grammars can generate arbitrarily deep nesting; parsing techniques and grammar rules can also address the dangling-else ambiguity.

  • Matching of parentheses: A classic context-free language (balanced parentheses) that a CFG can describe. For example, productions like S -> ( S ) S | ε generate all correctly matched parentheses strings.

  • Matching of function arguments: Cannot be enforced by a CFG alone. Verifying that the number and types of actual arguments match a function's parameter list needs semantic information (symbol tables and type information) and is performed during semantic analysis or via syntax-directed translation.

  • Declaration of a variable: Cannot be enforced by a CFG alone. Ensuring a variable is declared before use and handling scopes requires context-sensitive checks using a symbol table in the semantic analysis phase (for example, with SDT).

Cannot be captured by a CFG alone. Checking that the number and types of actual arguments match a function's parameter list requires semantic information (symbol table and type information) and is performed during semantic analysis or via syntax-directed translation, not by the CFG itself.

Cannot be captured by a CFG alone. Ensuring a variable is declared before use (and respecting scope) requires symbol-table lookups and scope rules performed in the semantic analysis phase (e.g., with SDT); this is context-sensitive and not enforceable by CFGs alone.

title: What is the space complexity of the CYK algorithm for
subject: Compiler Design
text: What is the space complexity of the CYK algorithm for the P table, where n is the number of words in the sentence and m is the number of non-terminal symbols in the grammar?
solution:
Concept: the space a dynamic-programming parser needs is (number of table cells) times (space one cell occupies). For a chart-parsing table the cells are indexed by the contiguous substrings, called spans, of the input, and each cell stores the set of grammar symbols that can derive that span - so the two factors are how many spans exist and how large a symbol set can be.

Application - CYK on a sentence of n words with a Chomsky-Normal-Form grammar of m non-terminals:

  1. The table P has one cell per span. A sentence of n words has n(n+1)/2 spans, which is O(n2) cells.

  2. Cell P[i, j] holds the set of non-terminals that derive the span starting at word i with length j. A set drawn from m non-terminals occupies O(m) space - m bits as a bit-vector, or at most m symbols as a list.

  3. Multiplying the two factors gives O(n2) times O(m) = O(n2m) for the whole P table.

Cross-check - what each of the four expressions actually counts:

Expression

What it counts

O(n3)

(start, split, end) index triples - the loop count behind CYK’s running time, not anything that is stored

O(nm2)

ordered non-terminal pairs (B, C) at each of n word positions - one span length, not all spans

O(n2m)

every span paired with every non-terminal - exactly the contents of the P table

O(n2m2)

every span paired with every ordered non-terminal pair - pairs are examined transiently while a cell is filled, they are not stored in it

Hence the P table occupies O(n2m) space. The often-quoted O(n3·|G|) figure is CYK’s time complexity, driven by the extra split-point loop, and must not be confused with its storage.

This expression is the order of the number of (word position, ordered non-terminal pair) combinations over the sentence: the n word positions of a sentence of n words paired with the m2 ordered pairs (B, C) drawn from the grammar's m non-terminals.

This expression is the order of the number of (span, non-terminal) combinations over the sentence: the n(n+1)/2 contiguous spans of a sentence of n words paired with the m non-terminals of the grammar.

solution: A recursive descent parser is a top-down parsing technique that builds the parse tree starting from the root node and working down to the leaves. title: Why must left recursion be eliminated in top-down parsers?
subject: Compiler Design
text: Why must left recursion be eliminated in top-down parsers?

options.html: It leads to ambiguity in the grammar
It slows down the execution of compiled programs
It cannot be represented using regular expressions

solution:
Top-down parsers, such as Recursive Descent and LL parsers, expand grammar rules recursively from the start symbol. If a grammar contains left recursion, a non-terminal immediately calls itself before consuming any input.

Example:

Expr → Expr + Term | Term

Here, Expr tries to expand into Expr + Term repeatedly, causing infinite recursion. Therefore, left recursion must be eliminated or converted into right recursion for successful top-down parsing.

Incorrect. The issue with left recursion is related to recursive parsing behavior, not regular expression representation.

solution:
In compiler design, a predictive top-down parser constructs the parse tree from the root node (the start symbol) down to the leaf nodes (the terminals/tokens) without ever rolling back or changing its mind.

To construct a deterministic parsing table for such a parser, the context-free grammar must satisfy the LL(1) properties:

  1. L: Left-to-right scanning of the input string.

  2. L: Leftmost derivation is used to construct the parse tree.

  3. (1): One token of lookahead is sufficient to make a non-backtracking decision.

For a grammar to be LL(1), it must not contain any Left-Recursion or Left-Factoring issues. When the parser looks at a non-terminal variable and the current lookahead token from the input, there must be exactly one valid production entry in the parsing table. If a grammar meets these mathematical conditions, the parser can predict the correct derivation path instantly, rendering backtracking completely unnecessary.

The 1 signifies that the parser looks ahead exactly one token to uniquely choose which production rule to apply.

solution:
Concept: A top-down (LL) parser must pick a production for a nonterminal using only the next input symbol, so a grammar can be an LL(1) grammar only if, at every nonterminal, no two alternatives can be triggered by the same lookahead symbol — and in particular, at most one alternative of a nonterminal may derive the empty string λ, since two alternatives that both reach λ create exactly such a clash.

For a concatenation language like { an bm cn+m }, the standard construction pairs the outer a/c layer with its own recursive nonterminal and hands off to a second nonterminal that generates the inner b/c layer down to λ, keeping the empty-string case reachable through exactly one path.

Application:

  1. Define S to generate the outer layer: S → aSc | S1. Peeling the aSc alternative n times gives an S1 cn.

  2. Define S1 to generate the inner layer: S1 → bS1c | λ. Peeling this m times gives bm cm.

  3. Substitute S1 = bm cm into an S1 cn: the result is an bm cm cn = an bm cn+m, matching L for every n, m ≥ 0 (including n = 0, or m = 0, or both).

  4. Check the lookahead sets at S: SELECT(S → aSc) = {a}; SELECT(S → S1) = {b} ∪ FOLLOW(S) = {b, c, $} (FOLLOW(S) includes c from the recursive aSc wrapping, plus end of input). These two sets are disjoint, so the choice at S is deterministic.

  5. Check the lookahead sets at S1: SELECT(S1 → bS1c) = {b}; SELECT(S1 → λ) = FOLLOW(S1) = {c, $}. These are disjoint too, so S1 is deterministic and the whole grammar S → aSc | S1, S1 → bS1c | λ is a valid LL(1) grammar.

solution:
Concept

Parser-class hierarchy: For the LR family, LR(0) ⊆ SLR(1) ⊆ LALR(1) ⊆ LR(1). A grammar is LR(0) when its LR(0) item-set (canonical collection) has no shift–reduce or reduce–reduce conflict in any state — i.e. no state holds a completed item [A → α·] together with a shift item, and no state holds two completed items. Separately, a grammar with left recursion (e.g. L → L , S) can never be LL(1).

Application to this grammar

  1. LL(1) check: The production L → L , S is immediately left-recursive, so the grammar is not LL(1). Any statement asserting LL(1) is therefore false.

  2. Build the LR(0) item sets. Augment the grammar with S′ → S and walk CLOSURE/GOTO state by state (dot · marks how far each item has been matched):

  1. I0 = {S′ → ·S, S → ·(L), S → ·a} — no completed item; pure shift/goto state.

  2. On '(' from I0: I2 = {S → (·L), L → ·L,S, L → ·S, S → ·(L), S → ·a} — no completed item; pure shift/goto state.

  3. On S from I2: I5 = {L → S·} — the only item in this state, so it is reduce-only; no shift item shares the state, hence no shift–reduce conflict.

  4. On L from I2: I4 = {S → (L·), L → L·,S} — both items have the dot immediately before a terminal (either ')' or ','), so this is a pure shift state with no completed item.

  5. On ')' from I4: I6 = {S → (L)·} — single completed item, reduce-only.

  6. On ',' from I4: I7 = {L → L,·S, S → ·(L), S → ·a} — no completed item; pure shift/goto state.

  7. On S from I7: I8 = {L → L,S·} — single completed item, reduce-only.

  8. On 'a' (from I0, I2, or I7): I3 = {S → a·} — single completed item, reduce-only.

  9. On S from I0: I1 = {S′ → S·} — the accept state.

Across all nine states, every state is either a pure shift/goto state (no completed item) or holds exactly one completed item (reduce-only) — no state ever mixes a completed item with a shift, and no state holds two completed items. So there is no LR(0) conflict anywhere: the grammar is LR(0).

Cross-check

Because LR(0) ⊆ SLR(1) ⊆ LR(1), an LR(0) grammar is automatically SLR(1) and LR(1) too — FOLLOW(L) = { ) , , } and FOLLOW(S) = { $ , ) , , } are never even needed to resolve a conflict, since none exists. Among the four statements, the only one consistent with “LR(0) = yes, LL(1) = no” is “The grammar can be parsed by LR(0) parser”. The word “only” is loose — every LR(0) grammar is trivially also SLR/LALR/LR(1) — but it is the intended reading, since it is the lone option that does not contradict the automaton just built.

A bare LR(0) parser, with zero lookahead, handles the whole grammar without any conflict. (The word “only” is technically loose, since any LR(0) grammar is automatically also SLR(1)/LALR(1)/LR(1).)

This claim rests on a presumed shift–reduce conflict in the zero-lookahead bottom-up tables that would supposedly need SLR FOLLOW-set lookahead to break. That premise comes from misreading the canonical item sets — pairing the completed item L → S· with a shift that does not actually share its state. Once the collection is drawn correctly, the supposed conflict this option depends on is simply not present.

This asserts LL(1), but the rule L → L , S is immediately left-recursive, and a top-down LL(1) parser cannot handle left recursion — it would recurse on L without consuming input. The LL(1) half of this statement therefore fails, regardless of the bottom-up part.

This labels the grammar LL(1), ignoring the immediate left recursion in L → L , S. Left recursion is exactly what an LL(1) parser cannot process, so the grammar is not LL(1) and “LL(1) only” cannot hold.

title: What is the difference between top-down and bottom-up parsing
subject: Compiler Design
text: What is the difference between top-down and bottom-up parsing?

options.html: Top-down parsing starts from the start symbol/root, while bottom-up parsing starts from the input symbols/leaves.
Top-down verifies rules against previous tokens, bottom-up constructs the parse tree
Top-down is more efficient for smaller grammars, bottom-up for larger ones

solution:
Top-down and bottom-up parsing differ mainly in the direction in which the parse tree is constructed.

In top-down parsing, the parser starts from the start symbol/root of the grammar and expands productions until it matches the input string. It builds the parse tree from root to leaves.

In bottom-up parsing, the parser starts from the input symbols/leaves and repeatedly reduces substrings to non-terminals until it reaches the start symbol. It builds the parse tree from leaves to root.

Hence, the correct answer is: Top-down parsing starts from the start symbol/root, while bottom-up parsing starts from the input symbols/leaves.

title: What type of grammar can be used for both top-down
subject: Compiler Design
text: What type of grammar can be used for both top-down and bottom-up parsing ?
solution: A Context-Free Grammar (CFG) is the broad class of grammars that encompasses both top-down and bottom-up parsing techniques. While specific subsets like LL(1) are designed exclusively for top-down parsing and LR(0) is strictly for bottom-up parsing, the general CFG definition does not restrict itself to one direction. Top-down parsers (like recursive descent) build the parse tree from the root down, whereas bottom-up parsers (like shift-reduce) construct it from leaves up. Since any grammar that can be parsed by either method must fundamentally adhere to the rules of a Context-Free Grammar, CFG is the correct classification. Therefore, Option C is the right answer because it represents the superset capable of supporting both parsing strategies depending on the specific algorithm chosen.

optionFeedback.html: An LL(1) grammar is a highly restrictive subset of CFG specifically engineered for top-down parsing. An LL(1) parser cannot handle grammars with left-recursion or non-factored productions, and it cannot be parsed by standard bottom-up engines without modification.

LR(0) grammars are designed specifically for bottom-up parsing using shift-reduce techniques. They cannot support top-down parsing because they lack the necessary lookahead and prediction capabilities required for predictive strategies.

A Context-Free Grammar is the overarching formal language framework used to define the syntax of programming languages. It specifies what strings belong to a language, completely independent of how a parser processes them. Both top-down parsers (like LL) and bottom-up parsers (like LR, SLR, LALR) operate on subsets of CFGs.

title: What is the maximum number of reduce moves that can
subject: Compiler Design
text: What is the maximum number of reduce moves that can be taken by a bottom-up parser for a grammar with no epsilon- and unit-production (i.e., of type A → ε and A → a) to parse a string with n tokens?
solution:
Concept

In a bottom-up (shift-reduce) parser, every reduce move replaces the right-hand side of a production by its left-hand-side non-terminal. When the grammar has NO unit productions (A → a, i.e. RHS of length 1) and NO epsilon productions (A → ε, RHS of length 0), every production used in a reduction has a right-hand side of length at least 2. So each reduce move consumes at least two stack symbols and produces exactly one — a strict net decrease of at least one symbol per reduce.

Application

We start with the n tokens of the input on the stack and must collapse them down to the single start symbol. Count the reductions when each reduction is as small as possible (binary, A → B C), which maximises their number:

  1. Begin with n symbols that must eventually become 1 (the start symbol).

  2. Because there are no unit/epsilon productions, every reduce takes at least 2 symbols and yields 1, so each reduce lowers the symbol count by at least 1.

  3. To go from n symbols down to 1, the total decrease needed is n − 1.

  4. Each reduce gives a decrease of at least 1, so the number of reduce moves can be at most n − 1.

  5. This bound is achieved exactly when every production is binary (A → B C): n − 1 such reductions turn n tokens into the start symbol.

Therefore the maximum number of reduce moves is n − 1.

Cross-check

Take a concrete string of n = 4 tokens, say p p q q, with a binary grammar. Reducing two adjacent symbols at a time: 4 → 3 → 2 → 1, which is exactly 3 reductions, and 3 = 4 − 1 = n − 1. The bound 2n − 1 would require reductions that each remove fewer than one symbol on average (impossible here), while 2n grows far too fast and n/2 is far too small.

optionFeedback.html: Halving the token count assumes each reduce can swallow a large group of symbols at once, as if productions had long right-hand sides. The grammar here gives no such guarantee, so a count proportional to half the tokens is far too small for the worst case the question asks about.

With no unit or epsilon productions, every reduce takes at least two symbols and produces one, so removing each net symbol on the way from the n input tokens to the single start symbol costs exactly one reduction. The total is therefore one fewer than the token count, attained when every production is binary (A → B C) — the tight maximum.

This value comes from tallying every parser action — both the shifts that read the input and the reductions — and reporting the combined activity. The question, however, asks for reductions alone. Bundling the input-reading steps into the same count is a category error that inflates the figure beyond the reductions actually performed.

The value 2ⁿ is exponential in n and corresponds to a count of possible parse states or trees, not parser actions. The number of reduce moves on a single string grows linearly with the input, so an exponential figure is far too large.

title: Which of the following correctly describes feature of Simple LR
subject: Compiler Design
text: Which of the following correctly describes a feature of Simple LR (SLR) parsing?

options.html: Parsing tables are not used in the SLR technique.
SLR parsing constructs a leftmost derivation of the input string.
FOLLOW sets are used in constructing SLR parsing tables.
SLR parsers rely on backtracking to analyse input strings.

solution:
SLR(1) parsing is a bottom-up (shift-reduce) LR technique: it builds an LR(0) automaton from the grammar's items and then places its reduce actions using FOLLOW sets computed from the grammar -- a reduce-by-A entry is added only under the terminals in FOLLOW(A) for a completed item A → α•. (If a shift-reduce or reduce-reduce conflict still remains after this, the grammar is not SLR(1).) This FOLLOW-set step is exactly what separates SLR from a plain LR(0) parser and from the stronger canonical-LR(1)/LALR(1) parsers, which instead compute per-state, context-sensitive lookaheads.

Building the SLR parsing table therefore means: for every LR(0) state containing a completed item A → α•, a reduce-by-that-production action is added in every ACTION-table column headed by a terminal in FOLLOW(A). This is precisely the feature that correctly describes SLR parsing among the options given.

Each of the other statements fails for a specific reason:

  • Claiming parsing tables are not used contradicts the core SLR mechanism -- SLR is entirely table-driven, using ACTION and GOTO tables built from the LR(0) automaton.

  • Claiming a leftmost derivation is constructed describes top-down (LL) parsing, not SLR -- every bottom-up/LR-family parser, SLR included, instead produces a rightmost derivation of the input in reverse.

  • Claiming SLR relies on backtracking is false -- its table-driven shift/reduce decisions are fully deterministic, so no backtracking over the input is ever needed.

So the FOLLOW-set-based reduce-action rule is the feature that correctly describes SLR parsing.

optionFeedback.html: SLR parsing is entirely table-driven: its ACTION and GOTO tables, built from the LR(0) automaton, are exactly how shift and reduce decisions are made, so parsing tables are central to the technique, not absent from it.

Constructing a leftmost derivation is a top-down (LL) parsing trait. SLR, like every bottom-up LR-family parser, instead produces a rightmost derivation of the input in reverse as it shifts and reduces.

FOLLOW sets are exactly how SLR resolves reduce actions: for every state containing a completed item, a reduce action is added under each terminal in FOLLOW of that production's left side, and this FOLLOW-set step is what distinguishes SLR from LR(0) and from the lookahead-based canonical-LR/LALR construction.
SLR's parsing decisions come directly from precomputed ACTION/GOTO table entries, so the parse proceeds deterministically in one pass; no backtracking over the input is ever required.

title: Which derivation is also known as canonical derivations?

text: Which derivation is also known as canonical derivations?
solution:
In the Theory of Computation and Compiler Design, formal languages use context-free grammars to derive strings. A derivation is a sequence of production steps that replaces non-terminals with terminal/non-terminal strings.

  • Rightmost Derivation (RMD): At each step of the derivation sequence, the rightmost non-terminal in the current sentential form is strictly chosen and replaced first.

  • Canonical Derivation: By formal computer science definition, a Rightmost Derivation is uniquely termed a Canonical Derivation. This specific relationship forms the structural foundation for bottom-up parsing techniques (like LR parsers), which implicitly trace a rightmost derivation in reverse order.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. Tracing a leftmost derivation in reverse does not equal a canonical derivation, nor does it correspond to a standard parsing sequence used by traditional parser families.

Correct. As defined in standard compiler theory text, a canonical derivation refers exclusively to a rightmost derivation.

Incorrect. A rightmost derivation in reverse represents the exact sequence of actions executed by a Bottom-Up Parser (such as an LR parser handles handle-pruning). While highly important, the reverse sequence itself is not named the canonical derivation; the original rightmost sequence holds that title.

CONCEPT: A state in the canonical LR(0) automaton carries a shift-reduce or reduce-reduce conflict only when TWO DIFFERENT items in that SAME state compete for the same lookahead symbol. SLR(1) restricts each reduce action to the lookaheads in FOLLOW of the reduced nonterminal — one GLOBAL, context-blind set covering every place that nonterminal ever appears in the grammar. LALR(1) instead computes, per state, the precise lookaheads a valid derivation can actually deliver there, which is never broader than FOLLOW (FOLLOW is the union across every context, not just the ones reaching this one state) — so wherever SLR(1)'s coarser FOLLOW-based check already avoids a clash in a state, LALR(1)'s narrower, state-specific lookaheads cannot manufacture a new clash there. So if a state in this grammar's LR(0) automaton never holds more than one completed item, and never holds a completed item alongside a shift action on the same symbol, there is only ONE production's item present to begin with — no amount of lookahead splitting can introduce a second, competing item into that state, so both SLR(1) and LALR(1) succeed there.

APPLICATION:

  1. FOLLOW(A): A occurs in S → Aa (followed by 'a') and S → bAc (followed by 'c'), so FOLLOW(A) = {a, c}.

  2. Build the canonical LR(0) item sets. The start state contains S′→•S, S→•Aa, S→•bAc, S→•dc, S→•bda, A→•a.

  3. On symbol 'a' from the start state, the automaton moves to the state {A→a•} — a single completed item with no other item sharing that state.

  4. After prefix 'b', the state {S→b•Ac, S→b•da, A→•a} also transitions on 'a' to that SAME state {A→a•} (identical item set), so the two paths converge on one state instead of colliding inside it.

  5. Every other position that completes a handle — {S→Aa•}, {S→dc•}, {S→bAc•}, {S→bda•} — is likewise reached as a state containing exactly that one completed item, with no shift action or second reduce competing for any symbol in that same state.

  6. So no state in the LR(0) automaton ever holds two competing actions on the same input symbol — the construction has zero shift-reduce or reduce-reduce conflicts even before any lookahead restriction is applied.

CROSS-CHECK: Every reduce-bearing state found above — {A→a•}, {S→Aa•}, {S→dc•}, {S→bAc•}, {S→bda•} — carries exactly one item, so there is never a second, competing item for LALR(1)'s finer per-state lookaheads to clash with. The FOLLOW(A) = {a, c} overlap only matters when it forces two DIFFERENT items into the same state, which never happens here. So the grammar succeeds under SLR(1) (the coarser check), and therefore also under LALR(1), whose lookaheads are never broader than SLR(1)'s.

Result: the grammar is parsable by both SLR(1) and LALR(1).

optionFeedback.html: This reading treats the FOLLOW(A) = {a, c} overlap as automatic proof that no amount of lookahead can disambiguate the state reached after processing prefix 'b' — but that overlap only forces a genuine clash when it lands two DIFFERENT completed items in the very same state. Tracing where the automaton actually goes on 'a' (both directly and after 'b') shows only one completed item ever occupies that state, so the overlap alone does not establish the failure this reading assumes.

This reading treats the FOLLOW(A) = {a, c} overlap as automatic proof that the simpler, FOLLOW-set-restricted method must fail here — but that overlap only forces a genuine clash when it lands two DIFFERENT completed items in the very same state. Tracing where the automaton actually goes on 'a' (both directly and after prefix 'b') shows only one completed item ever occupies that state, so the overlap alone does not establish the failure this reading assumes for that method.

The more powerful parsing method's per-state lookaheads are never broader than the simpler, FOLLOW-set-restricted method's lookaheads — if anything they are narrower, since they reflect only the contexts that actually reach a given state rather than every context the nonterminal appears in anywhere. So wherever the simpler method already avoids a clash in a state, the more powerful one cannot be tripped into a new clash there. A grammar accepted by the simpler method is therefore always also accepted by the more powerful one; this particular pairing (accepted by the simpler method only) can never occur for any grammar.

Every state of the canonical LR(0) automaton for this grammar contains at most one completed item, and no completed item ever shares a state with a shift action on the same symbol. Because each such state holds only one item to begin with, LALR(1)'s finer per-state lookaheads — never broader than SLR(1)'s FOLLOW-based lookaheads — have no second, competing item to clash with there either. The grammar is therefore conflict-free under both: parsable by SLR(1), and, since LALR(1) never needs a broader lookahead than SLR(1) already uses, by LALR(1) as well.

  • Rule iii (A → BaC): Valid. Variables are separated by terminal a.

  • Rule iv (A → ε): Violates condition 1 due to the null production.

Thus, i and iv violate the requirements.

title: Consider the following program: int main() int switch case printf("One\n");
subject: Compiler Design
text:
Consider the following C program:
int main() {

    int x = 5;

    switch (x + 1.5) {  

        case 1:

            printf("One\n");

            break;

        case 2:

            int y = x;  

            break;

        case 1:  

            printf("Duplicate\n");

            break;

        default:

            extern int z;  

            z = 10;

    }

    return 0;

}

Assume a standard two-pass compiler for C where type checking, scoping, and uniqueness constraints are handled post-parsing. The primary error in this program that prevents successful compilation is detected during which phase?
solution:
Correct phase: Semantic Analysis

Reason: Lexical analysis and syntax analysis would accept the program tokens and grammar. The errors that prevent successful compilation are detected by type checking, scope/unicity checks, and constant evaluation — all performed during semantic analysis.

  • Non-integer controlling expression: The expression x + 1.5 has a floating-point type. In C the switch controlling expression must have an integral type; using a floating type is a semantic (type-checking) error detected after parsing.

  • Duplicate case label: The same case constant appears more than once (case 1 is repeated). Duplicate case labels within the same switch are a uniqueness/scoping error caught during semantic analysis.

Conclusion: Both the non-integral switch expression and the duplicate case labels are semantic errors detected in the semantic-analysis phase, so compilation fails at that phase.

optionFeedback.html: Lexical analysis only breaks the source into tokens and reports malformed tokens or invalid characters. This program contains valid tokens, so lexical analysis would not catch the primary problems (type and duplicate-label issues). Those are detected later during semantic checks.

Syntax analysis verifies that tokens form grammatically valid constructs (e.g., correct placement of switch, case, braces, semicolons). The code is syntactically well-formed, so syntax analysis would not report the primary error. The errors here are type- and uniqueness-related and are caught during semantic analysis.

Semantic analysis performs type checking, scope resolution, and uniqueness checks. The switch controlling expression (x + 1.5) has a floating-point type, and C requires an integral controlling expression; additionally, there are duplicate case labels with the same constant value. These violations are semantic errors detected during semantic analysis, which is why compilation fails at that phase.

This program does have compile-time errors, so 'None of these' is incorrect. The relevant errors (non-integral switch expression and duplicate case labels) are detected during semantic analysis, not at some other phase.

Answer: The odd one out is the sequence "c 6 b / 36 + 9 9" because it is not a valid expression under the given grammar.

Token mapping: a = '*', b = '/', c = '+', d = '-', num = numeric literal

How to check validity (prefix binary operators):

  • Use an arity-count method: start with need = 1. For each token from left to right: if token is an operator (a, b, c, d) do need = need - 1 + 2 (net +1). If token is a number do need = need - 1. A valid expression finishes with need = 0.

  • "d a 4 10 a 4 10": valid. Need progression: 1 -> 2 (d) -> 3 (a) -> 2 (4) -> 1 (10) -> 2 (a) -> 1 (4) -> 0 (10).

  • "c b c 6 3 9 9": valid. Need progression: 1 -> 2 (c) -> 3 (b) -> 4 (c) -> 3 (6) -> 2 (3) -> 1 (9) -> 0 (9).

Conclusion: The sequence "c 6 b / 36 + 9 9" is the odd one out because it does not conform to the grammar terminals and fails the prefix arity check; the other three sequences are valid parses.

text:
Consider the SDT:

The SDT:

options.html: Counts the total number of x’s and y’s

solution:
Given SDT:

S → x S y {S.val = S.val + 2} | y S x {S.val = S.val + 2} | ε {S.val = 0}

Key idea:

  • Base case: ε sets S.val = 0.

  • Each use of a recursive production adds one x and one y and increments S.val by 2.

  • Therefore S.val equals 2 times the number of recursive expansions, which is exactly the total number of x and y symbols in the derived string.

Example: Consider the string x x y x y y (six terminals). The derivation requires three recursive expansions, so S.val = 0 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 6, which equals the total number of x's and y's.

title: Consider the statements: SDT embeds program fragments (also called semantic
subject: Compiler Design
text:
Consider the statements:

S1: SDT embeds program fragments (also called semantic actions) within production body.

S2: In SDT, the execution of semantic action is independent of its position within a production body.

Which of the above statement is/are TRUE?
solution:
Answer: Only S1 is true; S2 is false.

Explanation: SDD (Syntax-Directed Definitions) associates attributes and semantic rules with productions as a theoretical specification. SDT (Syntax-Directed Translation) implements these rules by embedding program fragments (semantic actions) directly in production bodies.

Why the first statement is true:

  • SDT embeds semantic actions inside productions, so program fragments appear within the production body.

Why the second statement is false:

  • In SDT the execution time of a semantic action depends on its position in the production. An action placed after some symbols is executed only after those symbols have been matched during parsing.

  • Example: for a production like A -> B {action1} C {action2}, action1 runs after B is matched, while action2 runs later after C is matched; moving an action changes when it executes and what attribute values are available.

Therefore: S1 is true and S2 is false, so the correct choice is the one that states only the first statement is true.

optionFeedback.html: This is incorrect. While it is true that syntax-directed translation embeds semantic actions within productions, the second statement is false: the execution time of a semantic action depends on its position in the production. Therefore both statements are not true.

Correct. Syntax-directed translation embeds program fragments (semantic actions) inside production bodies, so the first statement is true. The second statement is false because the execution time of an action depends on where it appears in the production.

This is incorrect. The second statement claims that execution of a semantic action is independent of its position, but in practice the execution time depends on where the action appears in the production. Also, the first statement is true, so it is not the case that only the second statement is true.

This is incorrect. The first statement is true: semantic actions are embedded in production bodies in syntax-directed translation. The second statement is false because the position of an action in the production determines when it runs during parsing.

title: Which of the following is/are true for symbol table
subject: Compiler Design
text: Which of the following is/are true for symbol table ?

options.html: Lexical analyzer only stores value in the symbol table.
Syntax analyzer only stores information in the symbol table.
Semantic analyzer stores and fetch information present in the symbol table.
Intermediate code generator only fetches information from symbol table.

solution:
Revised solution: Only the statement about the semantic analyzer is correct; the other statements are inaccurate as worded.

  • "Lexical analyzer only stores value in the symbol table."

    Evaluation: False. The lexical analyzer does not only store value; it recognizes tokens and often enters identifiers and literals into the symbol table with their lexeme and token type, and may record literal values. Additional attributes are added by later phases.

  • "Syntax analyzer only stores information in the symbol table."

    Evaluation: False. The syntax analyzer primarily builds and checks the syntactic structure; it may consult and add scope- or reference-related information to the symbol table, but it does more than just store information.

  • "Semantic analyzer stores and fetch information present in the symbol table."

    Evaluation: True. The semantic analyzer both retrieves information from the symbol table (for type and declaration checks) and stores semantic attributes (such as resolved types, bindings and other attribute information).

  • "Intermediate code generator only fetches information from symbol table."

    Evaluation: False. The intermediate code generator does fetch information (addresses, types, sizes) from the symbol table, but it may also create entries for temporaries or record intermediate results and their attributes.

Summary: The correct statement is the one describing the semantic analyzer's use of the symbol table. The other statements are incorrect because they assert an exclusive or incomplete role using the word "only" or are otherwise imprecise.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. The lexical analyzer does not "only" store the value in the symbol table. It typically recognizes tokens and may enter identifiers and literals into the symbol table with their lexeme, token type and literal value; additional attributes (like data type, scope, memory location) are added later by later phases.

Incorrect. The syntax analyzer does not "only" store information in the symbol table. Its primary role is to check and build the syntactic structure; it may consult and augment the symbol table (for example, to note scope or declarations), but it also primarily performs parsing rather than solely storing data.

Correct. The semantic analyzer both fetches information from and stores attribute information into the symbol table (for example, type information, bindings, and other attributes used for type checking and semantic checks).

Incorrect. The intermediate code generator does not only fetch information from the symbol table. It typically fetches information (addresses, types, sizes) but may also create entries for temporaries or record intermediate results and their attributes in the symbol table or a related table.

title: Consider the following statements. Parser can access symbol table in

text:
Question: Consider the following statements.
1. Parser can access symbol table in compiler
2. Parser uses stack for verifying syntax
3. Semantic analyzer can access symbol table in compiler
4. Semantic analyzer uses type information for type checking
Which of the above statements are TRUE?
solution:
a. True. The parser often needs to access the symbol table to resolve symbols and their attributes during the parsing process.
b. True. Parsers, particularly those implementing pushdown automata (such as LL and LR parsers), use stacks to keep track of grammar rules and syntax verification.
c. True. The semantic analyzer must access the symbol table to perform tasks such as type checking, scope resolution, and verifying other semantic rules.
d. True. One of the main responsibilities of the semantic analyzer is to use type information from the symbol table to ensure that operations in the program are semantically correct

optionFeedback.html: Statement 1 is true. In many compiler implementations the parser may consult the symbol table to resolve identifiers or attach attributes needed during parsing (for example to distinguish typedef names from ordinary identifiers). Note that while some symbol-table work is done during parsing, more extensive checks are usually handled later by the semantic analyzer.
Statement 2 is true. Parsers such as LL and LR are based on pushdown automata and use a stack to track grammar symbols and parser states while verifying the input's syntax.

title: What is the significance of the front-end phase in the

options.html: It allocates memory to executable code during program loading.
It interprets runtime errors and suggests fixes.
It analyzes source code for syntax and semantics to generate intermediate representation.
It schedules CPU instructions for faster execution.

solution:
The front-end phase is significant as it performs lexical, syntax, and semantic analysis to translate source code into an intermediate representation.

  1. Lexical Analysis: Grouping characters into tokens.

  2. Syntax Analysis: Checking structural rules and building a parse tree.

  3. Semantic Analysis: Checking type safety and logical constraints.

Once verified, it translates this source code into an Intermediate Representation (IR), which acts as a bridge for the back-end to optimize and turn into target machine code.

incorrect. The front-end phase catches compile-time errors (like syntax mistakes or type mismatches). It has no role in managing runtime errors, which occur long after compilation is complete when the program is actually executing.

Correct. The compiler construction process is split into two main parts: the Front-End (machine-independent) and the Back-End (machine-dependent). The front-end's sole responsibility is to analyze the source code for correctness and understand its meaning. It includes:

incorrect. Instruction scheduling and code optimization for target hardware performance are core responsibilities of the Back-End phase (specifically the code generator and optimizer), as these tasks require intimate knowledge of the specific target CPU architecture.

Synthesized attribute: A synthesized attribute at node N is defined only in terms of attribute values at the children of N and at N itself.

Inherited attribute: An inherited attribute at node N is defined only in terms of attribute values at N's parent, N itself, and N's siblings.

  • For the production P → Q R with the semantic rule Q.val = R.val: Q.val is an inherited attribute. This assignment defines Q.val using its sibling R (the rule is given at the parent), so Q.val depends on a sibling value and is therefore inherited.

  • For the production A → B C with the semantic rule A.val = B.val × C.val: A.val is a synthesized attribute. It is computed from the attribute values of its children B and C, so A.val is synthesized.

Conclusion: Q.val is an inherited attribute and A.val is a synthesized attribute.

optionFeedback.html: Incorrect. Q.val is not synthesized. In the production P → Q R with semantic rule Q.val = R.val, Q.val is defined using its sibling R (the assignment is given at the parent), so Q.val is an inherited attribute. A.val is computed from its children B and C (A.val = B.val × C.val), so A.val is a synthesized attribute.

Incorrect. Q.val is not a synthesized attribute — it is inherited because the rule Q.val = R.val defines Q.val in terms of its sibling R at the parent production. A.val is computed from its children (A.val = B.val × C.val), so A.val is a synthesized attribute (and thus saying only that it is not inherited misses the correct classification).

Partially correct. Q.val is an inherited attribute because in P → Q R with Q.val = R.val, Q.val is defined from its sibling R at the parent. However, A.val is synthesized: the rule A.val = B.val × C.val computes A.val from its children B and C, so saying A.val is not synthesized is incorrect.

Correct. In P → Q R with Q.val = R.val, Q.val is defined using its sibling R (the assignment is given at the parent), so Q.val is an inherited attribute. In A → B C with A.val = B.val × C.val, A.val is computed from its children B and C, so A.val is a synthesized attribute.

title: Select the correct option: &Optimization
subject: Compiler Design
text: Select the correct option(s):

options.html: Every L-attributed attribute is also a synthesized attribute.
Every inherited attribute satisfies the L-attributed restriction.
A basic block is a sequence of instructions where control enters the sequence at the beginning and exits at the end.
Live variable analysis can be used for dead code elimination.

solution:
Concept: Each statement here names a formal definition from a different area of compiler theory. An L-attributed definition allows, for every attribute, either a synthesized attribute (computed bottom-up from the children's attributes) or an inherited attribute restricted to depend only on the parent and on symbols to its left in the same production — the class permits both kinds and places a specific dependency restriction only on inherited attributes. Separately, a basic block is a maximal sequence of consecutive instructions with a single entry point (the first instruction) and a single exit point (the last instruction), and live variable analysis is a backward data-flow analysis that finds, at each program point, which variables may still be read later — an assignment outside that live set can be dropped as dead code.

  1. "Every L-attributed attribute is also a synthesized attribute" is false: the L-attributed class explicitly includes restricted inherited attributes alongside synthesized ones, so membership in the class does not force an attribute to be synthesized.

  2. "Every inherited attribute satisfies the L-attributed restriction" is false: an inherited attribute is L-attributed only when its dependencies are limited to the parent and left siblings; an inherited attribute that reads a right sibling's attribute (a common pattern in general attribute grammars) violates this restriction and is not L-attributed.

  3. "A basic block is a sequence of instructions where control enters at the beginning and exits at the end" is true: this is precisely the textbook definition — single entry at the first instruction, single exit at the last, with no internal branch targets or branch-causing instructions in between.

  4. "Live variable analysis can be used for dead code elimination" is true: once live variable analysis determines a variable is not live immediately after an assignment (and the assignment's right-hand side has no other externally observable effect), the optimizer can treat that assignment as dead code and remove it — this is exactly how live-variable data flow feeds dead-code elimination.

Cross-check: The two false statements both mishandle the direction of a subset relationship in L-attributed grammar theory (synthesized-in-L-attributed and inherited-in-L-attributed are not "every member automatically qualifies" claims), while the two true statements are independent, standard definitions from code optimization that hold without exception. Hence the correct options are the basic-block definition and the live-variable-analysis/dead-code-elimination statement.

optionFeedback.html: In a syntax-directed definition a synthesized attribute of a node is computed from the attributes of that node's children, while an inherited attribute is computed from attributes of the node's parent and its sibling symbols; an L-attributed definition additionally constrains each inherited attribute to depend only on the parent and on symbols to its left in the production.

A left-to-right evaluation order, of the kind an L-attributed definition imposes, allows a semantic rule to reference the parent and symbols positioned earlier in the same production; attribute grammars in general permit a semantic rule to reference other combinations of symbols as well.

Basic blocks are the compiler's unit for local, straight-line optimization; each one groups together a maximal run of instructions between two points where control transfer can occur, so that intra-block optimizations can be applied without worrying about branches interrupting the sequence.

Live variable analysis is a backward data-flow analysis that determines, at each program point, the set of variables whose current value may still be read later; a variable that is not in that live set immediately after an assignment holds a value that no subsequent instruction consumes.

title: UGC NET Computer Science and Applications Paper II - December 2009 - source Q33
subject: Compiler Design
text:
A shift-reduce parser carries out the actions specified within braces immediately after reducing with the corresponding rule of the grammar.

S → x x W  [print “1”]
S → y      [print “2”]
W → S z    [print “3”]

What is the translation of “x x x x y z z”?
solution:
Concept

In a syntax-directed translation attached to a bottom-up (shift-reduce) parser, each semantic action written in braces after a production fires at the instant that production REDUCES a completed handle on the parse stack — not when its symbols are shifted. Because a bottom-up parser builds a rightmost derivation in reverse, the innermost (earliest-completed) handle always reduces first, so an action on a nested construct fires before the action on the production that encloses it.

Application

  1. Shift the terminals x, x, x, x, y onto the stack (no right-hand side is complete yet); once y is on top it alone is the full right-hand side of S → y, so reduce it to S and fire print "2" — action 1. Stack: x x x x S.

  2. Shift the next terminal, z; the top of the stack is now S z, the complete right-hand side of W → S z. Reduce it to W and fire print "3" — action 2. Stack: x x x x W.

  3. The rightmost two x's together with this W form x x W, the complete right-hand side of S → x x W. Reduce it to S and fire print "1" — action 3. Stack: x x S.

  4. Shift the final terminal, z; the top of the stack is again S z, matching W → S z. Reduce it to W and fire print "3" — action 4. Stack: x x W.

  5. The remaining two x's together with this W again form x x W, matching S → x x W. Reduce it to S and fire print "1" — action 5. Stack: S, the start symbol — the whole input is accepted.

Cross-check

Rebuilding the parsed string bottom-up from this same trace confirms it is the only valid parse: the innermost S is "y", so the first W = "y"+"z" = "yz"; the next S = "x x"+"yz" = "xxyz"; the next W = "xxyz"+"z" = "xxyzz"; the outer S = "x x"+"xxyzz" = "xxxxyzz" — exactly the given input.

A second, structural check: every application of S → x x W needs exactly one W beneath it, and every W comes from exactly one W → S z reduction, so a valid translation always has an equal count of "1"s and "3"s, plus exactly one extra "2" from the single base-case S → y that starts the chain. The sequence 2, 3, 1, 3, 1 has two 1's, two 3's, and one 2, satisfying both checks.

The translation printed, in the order the reductions fire, is 2, 3, 1, 3, 1 — i.e., "2 3 1 3 1".

optionFeedback.html: This sequence opens with 1 and closes with 1, a combination that — under the grammar's print-to-terminal correspondence (two x's per '1', one y per '2', one z per '3') — draws on six x's, one y, and one z for these five prints.

This sequence opens with 1 and closes with 3, a combination that — under the grammar's print-to-terminal correspondence (two x's per '1', one y per '2', one z per '3') — draws on four x's, one y, and two z's for these five prints.

This sequence opens with 2 and closes with 1, a combination that — under the grammar's print-to-terminal correspondence (two x's per '1', one y per '2', one z per '3') — draws on four x's, one y, and two z's for these five prints.

title: Choose the correct expression for the given below DAG. &Optimization

text: Choose the correct expression for the given below DAG.
solution:
Final expression: a + a*(b-c) + (b-c)*d

Explanation:

  • Compute the subexpression (b - c) once; the DAG reuses this value rather than recomputing it.

  • Form a*(b - c) by multiplying a with the reused (b - c).

  • Form (b - c)*d by multiplying d with the reused (b - c).

Why the other expressions are incorrect:

  • 'None of these' is incorrect because the correct expression appears among the provided choices.

title: What are the benefits of using intermediate code instead of
subject: Compiler Design

options.html: Allows for different code generation backends for various platforms
Simplifies the parsing and semantic analysis phases
Reduces the memory footprint of the compiler

solution:
The correct answer is 1) Allows for different code generation backends for various platforms.

Using Intermediate Representation (IR) is a fundamental strategy in modern compiler design (like LLVM or GCC) because it acts as a universal bridge between the source language and the target hardware.

Key Benefits of Intermediate Code

  • Portability: As mentioned, you can target new hardware (ARM, x86, RISC-V) just by swapping the back-end.

  • Machine-Independent Optimization: Most code optimizations (like removing "dead code" or simplifying math) are the same regardless of the CPU. IR allows the compiler to optimize once before reaching the hardware-specific stage.

  • Easier Debugging: IR is typically more human-readable than raw binary, making it easier for compiler developers to verify that the logic remains intact during the translation process.

Intermediate code does not simplify parsing or semantic analysis. These phases occur before intermediate code generation. Check the compiler pipeline stages to identify where parsing happens.

In fact, using intermediate code often increases the memory and time requirements of the compiler itself. The compiler has to perform extra steps to generate, store, and then process the IR. However, this "cost" is accepted because the resulting machine code is far more optimized and portable.

  • Constant folding — evaluate expressions involving known constants.

    c = y * c + b

  • Copy propagation — substitute the copy where it is used.

    c = y * c + y

  • Dead code elimination — remove assignments that are no longer needed.

    After propagation the assignments to x and z are unused and can be removed. The temporary b is also eliminated.

    Final optimized code (after these passes):

    y = 3 + a

    c = y * c + y

title: Which of the following concepts can be used to identify

solution:
Answer: All three concepts — Depth-first ordering, Dominators, and Reducible graphs — can be used to identify loops.

Key ideas:

  • Depth-first ordering: A DFS of the control-flow graph classifies edges and exposes back edges (edges to ancestors). Each back edge signals a loop and is used to form the natural loop around the loop header.

  • Dominators: Dominator analysis identifies nodes that must be passed to reach others; a back edge from a node to one of its dominators indicates a natural loop with that dominator as the unique loop header, and the dominator tree helps determine loop nesting.

  • Reducible graphs: If a control-flow graph is reducible, its loops are guaranteed to be natural (single-entry), which makes standard loop-detection techniques (based on back edges and dominators) correct and simpler to apply.
